section.title: The Jew and the Law
section.sectionRationale: Paul now names the moralist he has been addressing: the Jew who leans on the law, boasts in God, and is confident he is a guide to the blind. Paul grants every privilege, then presses a single devastating question: do you keep the law you teach? The one who boasts in the law dishonors God by breaking it, so that God's name is blasphemed among the nations. Circumcision in the flesh means nothing without obedience; true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code.
section.thesis: Covenant privilege, the possession of the law, and the outward mark of circumcision cannot save a person who breaks the law; God looks for a reality of the heart, an inward and Spirit-wrought devotion, and He gives His praise not to the outwardly religious but to the inwardly transformed.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the Jew who relies on the law and boasts in God; the searching questions that expose the teacher who does not practice what he preaches; and the redefinition of the true Jew and true circumcision as a matter of the heart, by the Spirit.

units.label: The Jew who relies on the law

verses.text: Now you, if you call yourself a {{Ioudaios|Jew}}; if you rely on the {{nomos|law}} and boast in God;
if you know His will and approve of what is superior because you are instructed by the law;
if you are convinced that you are a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness,
an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, because you have in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth:

units.label: You who teach others, do you not teach yourself?
units.note: the boast in the law contradicted by breaking it

verses.text: you, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal?
You who forbid adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?
As it is written: “God's name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

units.label: True circumcision is of the heart
units.note: inward and by the Spirit, not by the written code

verses.text: {{peritome|Circumcision}} has value if you observe the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.
If a man who is not circumcised keeps the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?
The one who is physically uncircumcised yet keeps the law will condemn you who, even though you have the written code and circumcision, are a lawbreaker.
A man is not a Jew because he is one outwardly, nor is circumcision only outward and physical.

No, a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the {{pneuma|Spirit}}, not by the {{gramma|written code}}. Such a man's praise does not come from men, but from God.

Ioudaios.gloss: A Jew, a member of the covenant people descended from Judah. Paul finally names the moralist he has been addressing. To be called a Jew was to claim a real and God-given privilege, but Paul will argue that the name carries no weight before God unless it is matched by an inward reality, redefining the true Jew as one inwardly, not merely by descent.

nomos.gloss: Law, especially the law of Moses, the Torah. The Jew relies on the law and boasts in possessing it. Paul does not deny its glory, but he insists that resting in the law without keeping it is worthless; the law he trusts becomes the very measure that condemns him as a lawbreaker.

peritome.gloss: Circumcision, the covenant sign given to Abraham, cut in the flesh of every Israelite male. Paul grants its value if the law is kept, but warns that a lawbreaker's circumcision counts as uncircumcision. The outward sign without the inward reality is empty; God seeks circumcision of the heart.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, here the Holy Spirit as the agent of true, inward circumcision. Real covenant membership is a work of the Spirit on the heart, not merely a mark on the body. This points forward to the new covenant, in which God writes His law within and gives His Spirit to His people.

gramma.gloss: Letter or written code, the law as external written instruction. Paul contrasts the mere letter with the Spirit: circumcision by the written code is outward and physical, but circumcision by the Spirit is inward and real. The letter can command but cannot transform; only the Spirit gives the changed heart God requires.

basic.context: Paul has been dismantling the confidence of the moralist who judges others while doing the same things. Now he addresses that person by name: the Jew who trusts in the law and the covenant. This was the person most likely to feel exempt from chapter 1's indictment, since Israel possessed the very words of God. Paul honors that privilege and then shows that privilege without obedience only deepens guilt.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage is built on a series of if clauses, verses 17 to 20, that list the Jew's real advantages, followed by a series of stinging questions, verses 21 to 23, that expose the gap between teaching and doing. Then Paul redefines Jew and circumcision, moving from the outward and physical to the inward and Spirit-wrought. Read the argument as a whole: privilege is real, but it does not exempt; it intensifies responsibility.
basic.originalLanguages: To be a Ioudaios, a Jew, and to hold the nomos, the law, were genuine privileges. But peritome, circumcision in the flesh, without obedience becomes uncircumcision. The true circumcision is by the pneuma, the Spirit, not by the gramma, the mere written code. God's praise falls on the inward reality, not the outward badge.
basic.typology: Circumcision of the flesh, the sign given to Abraham, points beyond itself to circumcision of the heart, promised in Deuteronomy and fulfilled by the Spirit in the new covenant. The physical sign was always meant to signify an inner cutting away of hardness and sin, and Paul insists the sign is empty without the substance.
basic.christ: Paul does not name Christ directly here, but the whole passage prepares for Him. The heart circumcised by the Spirit is the work of the new covenant that Christ inaugurates by His blood and pours out at Pentecost. The praise that comes from God, not from men, is granted only to those united to Christ, whose Spirit writes God's law within.
basic.god: God is not impressed by outward badges or inherited privileges. He looks on the heart, values obedience over profession, and reserves His praise for the inward and real. He is jealous for His own name, which is blasphemed among the nations when His people boast in the law yet break it. He seeks worshipers in Spirit and in truth.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that the LORD will circumcise your heart. Jeremiah 9:25-26 warns of those circumcised only in the flesh. Isaiah 52:5 laments that God's name is blasphemed among the nations. Philippians 3:3 declares that we are the circumcision who worship by the Spirit and put no confidence in the flesh.
basic.oneStory: God gave Israel the law and the covenant sign as precious gifts pointing to a deeper reality. The prophets had always warned that an uncircumcised heart made the outward sign empty. Paul now brings that warning to its climax: covenant privilege cannot save the disobedient, and the true people of God are those whose hearts the Spirit has circumcised, a people gathered in Christ from Jew and Gentile alike.

context.literary:
This section is the part of the argument where the unnamed 'you' of 2:1 finally receives a name. Verses 17 to 20 are one long sentence in Greek, a string of 'if' clauses that never reaches its conclusion. Paul piles up eight claims the Jewish teacher makes about himself: he bears the name Jew, rests on the law, boasts in God, knows His will, approves what is excellent, guides the blind, lights the dark and instructs the foolish. The sentence is left hanging. The main clause that should follow, something like 'then you ought to...', is never spoken, and verse 21 breaks in with questions. The grammar of the sentence is the argument: it climbs, and then falls.

Verses 21 to 24 are five rapid questions, built in pairs. 'You who teach others, do you not teach yourself?' is the thesis, and three examples follow from the commandments, stealing, adultery and temple robbery. The fifth question gathers them: 'You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?' Verse 24 then closes the section with a quotation from Isaiah as a verdict. The boasting of verses 17 and 23 and the dishonor of verse 23 and the blasphemy of verse 24 form a chain from privilege to disgrace.

Verses 25 to 29 move from conduct to the covenant sign. The topic changes from the law to circumcision, but the logic is unchanged. Paul reasons in three stages: circumcision with obedience has value, verse 25; uncircumcision with obedience is counted as circumcision, verses 26 and 27; and then he defines the true Jew, verses 28 and 29. The last two verses are tightly balanced pairs, outward and inward, flesh and heart, letter and Spirit, men and God.

The section is also a hinge. It completes the indictment of the Jew begun at 2:1, and it opens the objections of chapter 3, which begin with exactly the question this passage raises: 'What, then, is the advantage of being a Jew?' Romans 3:1.
context.historical:
To be a Jew in the Roman world was to belong to a people who were conspicuous. They kept the Sabbath, refused the worship of other gods, and followed food laws, and the men were circumcised. Circumcision was the badge that identified them, and it was often an object of ridicule among their neighbors. For the Jew it was the sign of the covenant that God made with Abraham, Genesis 17:10-14, and to be uncircumcised was to be outside it. The list in verses 17 to 20 describes a real self-image that Jewish teachers held, and a real calling. Israel had been told to be 'a light to the nations,' Isaiah 42:6-7, and the Jew who believed himself to be a guide of the blind was repeating the language of the prophets.

The charges of verses 21 and 22 were not invented for rhetoric. Jewish teachers of the time were well aware that hypocrisy was a danger, and Jesus Himself had called the Pharisees blind guides, Matthew 15:14 and 23:16. The question about robbing temples is the least obvious. The Jewish law forbade taking the silver and gold from the idols of the nations, Deuteronomy 7:25-26, and the town clerk at Ephesus said Paul's companions had 'neither robbed our temple nor blasphemed our goddess,' Acts 19:37, which suggests that the charge of temple robbery was a known accusation against Jews. The Jewish historian Josephus also reports a scandal in Rome when a Jewish teacher and his associates defrauded a Roman woman who had given gifts for the Jerusalem temple, with the result that Jews were expelled from the city. Paul may have such events in mind. The Roman church was shaped by memory of the expulsion in the time of Claudius, Acts 18:2.

The Jewish exile was the background of Isaiah 52:5. Israel had been carried into captivity, and the nations took her suffering to mean that her God was weak. Ezekiel says the same: wherever the people went they 'profaned My holy name,' because it was said, 'These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land,' Ezekiel 36:20. That is the history behind verse 24. Paul tells the Jew in Rome that the old pattern is being repeated.
context.canonical:
Circumcision was commanded in Genesis 17 as the sign of the covenant, and almost at once the Scriptures begin to say that the sign points beyond itself. Moses tells Israel, 'Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more,' Deuteronomy 10:16, and promises that the LORD will do it for them, 'The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants,' Deuteronomy 30:6. Jeremiah 4:4 repeats the call to remove 'the foreskins of your hearts.' Jeremiah 9:25-26 is the passage that Paul has most plainly in mind: God will punish all who are circumcised yet uncircumcised, listing Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon and Moab, and saying that 'the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart.' Leviticus 26:41 speaks of 'uncircumcised hearts' that must be humbled, and Ezekiel 44:7 complains of foreigners 'uncircumcised in both heart and flesh' in the sanctuary.

The Isaiah quotation also has a wide frame. Isaiah 52:5 comes at the opening of the great passage of comfort that ends with the suffering servant, Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12. Ezekiel 36:20-27 pairs the profaning of God's name among the nations with the promise of a new heart and a new spirit, 'I will put My Spirit within you,' Ezekiel 36:27. Paul's movement from name blasphemed in verse 24 to circumcision of the heart by the Spirit in verse 29 is that same movement.

The New Testament carries these themes forward. Stephen tells the council they are 'uncircumcised' in heart and ears, Acts 7:51. Paul says the Philippian believers are 'the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh,' Philippians 3:3, and tells the Colossians they were 'circumcised, in the putting off of your sinful nature, with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands,' Colossians 2:11. To the Galatians he says that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; 'What counts is a new creation,' Galatians 6:15. Romans 4 picks up the thread within this letter, saying Abraham received the sign of circumcision 'as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised,' Romans 4:11.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul addresses a Jewish teacher he respects. Nothing in these verses mocks the law or the covenant, and he will say in Romans 3:1-2 that the Jew's advantage is great and in 7:12 that the law is holy. His complaint is that the privilege has become a place to stand. The list in verses 17 to 20 is the real equipment of a faithful Jewish guide, and Paul chooses it for that reason. If he wanted to attack a caricature he would not have started by honoring the real thing.

His purpose is to show that the gap between teaching and doing is not a minor flaw. It is the failure that dishonors God in front of the world, and it is common to everyone who holds a standard higher than he lives. The questions of verses 21 to 23 are not cruel. They are the questions every honest teacher asks himself, and Paul does not exempt himself from them, for in 1 Corinthians 9:27 he says he disciplines his body so that after preaching to others he will not be disqualified.

The final verses show the direction of the argument. If circumcision cannot save the disobedient, then neither can any outward identity: not membership, not ancestry, not baptism or church attendance in later ages. The thing God wants is what He has always promised to give, a heart cut free from its hardness. Paul wants the Jewish reader to see that his own Scripture points that way, and he wants the Gentile reader to see that the promise belongs to him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes a failure, and it does so by asking questions, so it is easy to turn it into a stick. A better reading starts by noticing what Paul does not say. He does not say that all Jews steal and commit adultery. The questions are rhetorical and probe the danger of the position, not the record of every person. The 'you' is a representative, and the lesson is for any teacher or believer who holds a standard he does not keep.

What carries forward is a test of integrity for anyone who speaks about God: do I teach myself what I teach others? Jesus made the same point in Matthew 23:3, and James repeats it, 'we who teach will be judged more strictly,' James 3:1. The passage also carries forward a warning about identity markers. Any outward sign, whether circumcision then, or church membership, a confession, or a family tradition now, can become a place where trust rests that should rest on God. Paul's remedy is not to abolish the signs. Romans 4:11 says circumcision was a seal of faith. The remedy is to hold them as signs and not as substitutes.

The passage does not tell the church to treat Jewish people as hypocrites, nor does it say that Israel's election has ended. Paul writes in Romans 11:1-2 that God has not rejected His people. Readers who have used these verses against Jews have used them against the plain direction of the letter.

debates.question: Who is the uncircumcised man who keeps the law, verses 26 and 27?

views.label: A Gentile believer transformed by the Spirit
views.case: Many read this as a Gentile Christian, uncircumcised in the flesh but circumcised in the heart, whose obedience shames the disobedient Jew. This fits Paul's definition of the inward Jew in verse 29, and it matches Romans 8:4, where the law's righteous requirement is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit. Philippians 3:3 says believers are the circumcision.

views.label: A hypothetical or representative Gentile
views.case: Others take the man as hypothetical, a case that makes a logical point: if obedience is what counts, then uncircumcised obedience would outrank circumcised disobedience. This reading avoids the question of whether any Gentile fully keeps the law, and it fits Paul's grammar, which says 'if.'

views.label: Any Gentile who does what conscience requires
views.case: A third reading connects the verse with 2:14-15, where Gentiles do by nature what the law requires. The man is the Gentile who shows the work of the law written on his heart. Critics reply that Paul speaks here of 'keeping the requirements of the law,' which sounds like more than occasional moral instinct.

debates.bearing: On every reading Paul overturns the confidence placed in the circumcised flesh. What he praises is a heart that obeys, and the first view best explains how anyone can actually do that, by the Spirit, which is where verse 29 ends.

debates.question: Is the 'Spirit' of verse 29 the Holy Spirit or the human spirit?

views.label: The Holy Spirit
views.case: Paul contrasts 'Spirit' with 'letter' in the same way as 2 Corinthians 3:6, 'the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life,' and Romans 7:6, where believers serve 'in the new way of the Spirit.' Ezekiel 36:27 promises circumcision of heart by God's own Spirit. Most English translations capitalize the word for this reason.

views.label: The inward human spirit
views.case: A few scholars read the contrast as inner against outer within a person: a circumcision of the spirit as opposed to the flesh. They note that 2:28 and 29 describe the 'outward' and 'inward' and that Paul has not yet mentioned the Spirit in the letter.

debates.bearing: The first reading fits Paul's usage in the rest of Romans and the prophetic promise of a new heart. The second correctly sees that the point of the verse is inward reality, and the two views differ little in practice, since the inward change of the heart is what the Spirit does.

debates.question: Is Paul saying the church has replaced Israel as the 'true Jew'?

views.label: A redefinition that makes the church the true Israel
views.case: Some read verses 28 and 29 as saying that the true Jew is anyone, Jew or Gentile, with a circumcised heart, so that the name has moved from the nation to the church. They point to Galatians 3:29, 'if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed,' and to Philippians 3:3.

views.label: An inward test within Israel, not a transfer
views.case: Others observe that Paul's argument is a prophetic one, not a replacement theology. The prophets had said that not all in Israel were faithful. Paul does not say the church is Israel here, and in Romans 9:6 he says 'not all who are descended from Israel are Israel,' while in Romans 11:1 and 11:26 he continues to speak of Israel as a people God has not rejected.

debates.bearing: Paul's wording stays within Israel's own categories. He defines the inward Jew by the standard of Deuteronomy 30:6, and then in chapter 4 explains that Abraham is the father both of the circumcised who share his faith and of the uncircumcised who believe, Romans 4:11-12. The passage widens the family of promise without declaring that the nation's calling has ended.

debates.question: What does 'rob temples' mean in verse 22?

views.label: Taking treasure from pagan temples
views.case: The law forbade Jews to take the silver and gold of idols, Deuteronomy 7:25-26, and the town clerk of Ephesus defends Paul's companions on exactly this point, Acts 19:37. The charge would be that a Jew who abhors idols profits from them, the very sin of a man who is a hypocrite about his own standard.

views.label: Robbing God's temple
views.case: Malachi 3:8-9 says that withholding tithes is robbing God, and Jeremiah 7:9-11 accuses the people of stealing and committing adultery and then coming to the temple as if safe, making it 'a den of robbers.' On this view Paul means that the Jew desecrates the sanctuary he claims to honor.

views.label: A general illustration of hypocrisy
views.case: Others hold that Paul chose three sample sins without pointing to specific events. He sets theft, adultery and sacrilege as three typical failures, so that every hearer will recognize one he has committed.

debates.bearing: The first two readings fit known Jewish practice and Scripture, and the third is likely implied by both. In every case Paul's point is the same: one who forbids a sin must not do it.

study.originalLanguages:
The name Paul gives his reader in verse 17, Ioudaios, has a hidden meaning that Paul uses at the end of the passage. Leah named her fourth son Judah, saying 'This time I will praise the LORD,' Genesis 29:35, and Jacob blessed him, 'Judah, your brothers shall praise you,' Genesis 49:8. The name itself carries the sense of praise. So when Paul ends in verse 29 with 'Such a man's praise does not come from men, but from God,' the word for praise, epainos, rings against the name he began with. The Jew is the praised one, and the question is who does the praising.

In verse 17 the Jew 'relies on' the law, epanapauē nomō, a verb that means to rest upon, as on a bed or a support. He 'boasts' in God, kauchasai. Boasting in God is not wrong in itself. Jeremiah 9:23-24 says a man may boast 'that he understands and knows Me,' and the next verses of Jeremiah are the very warning about circumcision that Paul draws on. The word becomes dangerous when the boasting rests on possession of the law, since boasting is later excluded altogether, Romans 3:27.

The phrase in verse 18 translated 'approve of what is superior' is dokimazeis ta diapheronta, 'you test the things that differ.' The same dokim- family appears in 1:28, where the people did not 'see fit,' and an adokimos mind was the result. A Jew who tests rightly what differs is better placed than the pagan, and for that reason more accountable. Verse 18 also says he is 'instructed,' katechoumenos, the source of the English word catechism. Verse 20 calls the law the 'embodiment,' morphosis, of knowledge and truth, a word that means a form or outline. The law is the shape of the truth, and a shape can be held without possessing what it shapes.

The five questions of verses 21 to 23 turn on the verb 'dishonor,' atimazeis. In verse 23 the man who boasts in the law dishonors God by transgression, parabasis, a stepping across a line. Verse 24 gives the consequence as blasphemeitai, the name is 'blasphemed,' a passive verb that does not say who does the blaspheming, only that the cause is the people's conduct. Paul's wording follows the Greek Old Testament, which says that the name is blasphemed among the nations because of the people, while the Hebrew of Isaiah 52:5 says only that it is blasphemed continually.

In verses 26 and 27 the key verb is 'regarded,' logisthesetai, 'will be reckoned.' It is the accounting verb that Paul will use in chapter 4, where Abraham's faith was 'credited' to him as righteousness, 4:3, 4:9-10, and where the question is asked, 'Was it after his circumcision, or before?' 4:10. Here the verb is already doing the work of an accountant: circumcision and uncircumcision are entries in a ledger that God reads by the heart. In verse 27 the uncircumcised man 'will condemn' the transgressor, krinei, the judging verb of 2:1, so the Gentile who obeys becomes a witness against the Jew who does not. He does this 'even though you have the written code and circumcision,' where the preposition is best read as 'in spite of.'

The closing contrast sets gramma against pneuma, 'letter' against 'Spirit.' Gramma means what is written, the code as an external document that can instruct but not empower. The rare phrase 'in secret' in verse 29, en tō kryptō, joins the 'secrets,' krypta, that God judges at 2:16. What is hidden from men is what God sees and praises. 'The heart,' kardia, in the Hebrew Scriptures is the seat of will and not merely of feeling, and to circumcise it is to remove what blocks obedience.

typology.type: Circumcision of the flesh and of the heart, Genesis 17:10-14 and Deuteronomy 30:6
typology.fulfillment: The cut in the flesh marked every Israelite male as belonging to the covenant, and Moses already hinted at its inner meaning by calling for circumcised hearts. Paul says the substance has come: believers are circumcised 'with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands,' Colossians 2:11, and they worship 'by the Spirit of God,' Philippians 3:3. The correspondence is that both signs mean the removal of what separates from God. The escalation is that the new sign is wrought by Christ and received by faith in baptism, Colossians 2:12. The type is not rejected. Romans 4:11 says it was a seal of faith, and it fell short only when it was taken for the thing it signified.

typology.type: Israel as a light to the nations, Isaiah 42:6-7 and 49:6
typology.fulfillment: Israel was called to be a light and to open the eyes of the blind, and the 'guide of the blind' of verse 19 claims that office. Israel the Servant, however, 'labored in vain,' and the LORD says, 'It is not enough for You to be My Servant... I will also make You a light for the nations,' Isaiah 49:3-6. The calling comes to rest on one Servant who is true Israel. Simeon sees Him as 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel,' Luke 2:32, and Jesus says 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12. The type is partly fulfilled in His people, who are told to 'proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness,' 1 Peter 2:9.

typology.type: The temple robbed and the house of prayer, Jeremiah 7:9-11
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah accused Judah of living in theft and adultery and then coming to the temple as to a safe place, making it 'a den of robbers.' Jesus used the same words when He cleared the temple, Matthew 21:12-13, and the question 'do you rob temples?' stands behind His action. The escalation is that Jesus is Himself the temple that is destroyed and raised, John 2:19-21, so the final answer to a corrupted sanctuary is not a better building but a body in which God dwells. The type falls short only in that Jeremiah warned of destruction while Jesus accomplished the replacement.

typology.type: The law on stone and the law on the heart, Exodus 31:18 and Ezekiel 36:26-27
typology.fulfillment: The tablets of stone were written by God's finger, and the people who received them could not keep them. Paul says the church is 'a letter from Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts,' 2 Corinthians 3:3. The correspondence is the same Lawgiver and the same righteousness. The escalation is that the writing is now on the person, by the Spirit, which is what Ezekiel promised. The type is not a failure of the law, which Paul says is holy, Romans 7:12, but of a heart that could not obey it.

study.christ:
Christ is not named in these verses, and a reader who looks for Him should not invent a hint. What the passage does is expose a need that only He meets, and it uses categories He fulfills.

The first is the figure of the teacher who cannot do what he teaches. Jesus is the only teacher whose life matched His words. He said 'Learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart,' Matthew 11:29, and 'I have set you an example,' John 13:15, and He could ask His accusers, 'Which of you can prove Me guilty of sin?' John 8:46. Every other teacher of the law stands under the questions of verses 21 to 23. He alone can say 'I have kept My Father's commandments,' John 15:10. This is why Hebrews 7:26 says we have a high priest 'holy, innocent, undefiled.' The gap between profession and practice that Paul exposes is closed only in Him.

The second is the circumcision of the heart. Moses promised that the LORD Himself would do it, Deuteronomy 30:6. In Christ the promise is given. Paul says believers were 'circumcised... with the circumcision performed by Christ,' Colossians 2:11, and that the promise of the Spirit is received through Him, Galatians 3:14. Jesus Himself was circumcised on the eighth day, Luke 2:21, and was born 'under the law,' Galatians 4:4, so He took on the sign and carried its obligation, 'to redeem those under the law.' The hearts that Moses called Israel to circumcise are the hearts the risen Lord gives the Spirit to change, Ezekiel 36:26-27.

The third is the praise of God. The passage ends with the praise that comes 'not from men, but from God,' verse 29. In Jesus the Father says, 'This is My beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased,' Matthew 3:17, and those who are in Him share the Son's standing. Paul says each believer will receive his praise from God, 1 Corinthians 4:5, and he means praise purchased by Christ's obedience, not earned by theirs. The complaint of John 12:43, that some 'loved praise from men more than praise from God,' is the very trap Paul has set for the moralist.

Finally, Christ is the true Israel. Paul says in Romans 15:8 that Christ 'has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs.' Where the Jew of Romans 2 dishonors the name, Jesus says 'Father, glorify Your name,' John 12:28, and 'I have manifested Your name,' John 17:6. Where Israel failed to be a light to the nations, He is the light. The verses are a lawcourt, and the verdict will be answered by 3:21-26, where the righteousness of God is given through faith in Jesus Christ. A reading that makes the passage mainly a warning against Judaism misses that Paul is holding up a mirror to anyone who relies on religious identity, including a Christian who relies on baptism or church membership without a changed heart.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the one who gave the law and who still looks to see it kept. Paul does not suggest that Israel's privileges were an error. Those privileges came from God, and the law is His gift. The passage shows a God of faithful self-disclosure who had told Israel what He wanted in a form they could read, and who holds those who read it more accountable than those who did not.

He is a God who values the reality of obedience over the badge of belonging. This is not a New Testament novelty. When Samuel was sent to anoint a king, he was told that 'man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart,' 1 Samuel 16:7. The prophets had said the same about the temple sacrifices, Isaiah 1:11-17, and about circumcision, Jeremiah 9:25-26. Paul's ending, praise from God for what is inward and hidden, echoes Jesus' phrase in the Sermon on the Mount, 'your Father, who sees what is done in secret,' Matthew 6:4.

He is a God who cares about His name. The quotation in verse 24 speaks of a name that is blasphemed because of the conduct of the people who bear it, and Scripture treats this as a serious matter. The third commandment is about carrying the name of the LORD lightly, Exodus 20:7. In Ezekiel 36:22-23 He says He will act 'not for your sake... but for My holy name,' and show its holiness before the nations. This jealousy is not vanity. It is a concern that the world see the truth about Him, and it is bound to the way His people live.

He is a God who promises to change the heart. The same God who demands what He cannot find has said, 'I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes,' Ezekiel 36:26-27. The gap between what the law asks and what people give is not a trap. It is the setting for a gift. When Paul says in verse 29 that the true circumcision is by the Spirit, he points to God as the one who does what He commands.

He is a God who is faithful. Though some Israelites have failed, His word has not failed, as Romans 3:3-4 and 9:6 will say. The praise that He gives is real, and the people who receive it are real: those whose hearts He has changed.

For worship, the passage teaches humility before a God who looks at what is unseen. It also teaches confidence, because the God who sees the heart is the God who gives a new one, and a church can pray with Paul and David, 'Create in me a clean heart, O God,' Psalm 51:10.

crossReferences.note: The verses that Paul has most clearly in view. A man may boast in knowing the LORD, and then God warns of punishing all who are circumcised yet uncircumcised, naming Egypt, Judah and others, since 'the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart.' Paul's sequence of boasting, then circumcision, follows this passage.

Moses commands, 'Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more.' The inner circumcision of Romans 2:29 was always part of the Law's own demand, so Paul is not replacing Moses but reading him.

The LORD Himself will circumcise the hearts of the people and their descendants so that they will love Him. Verse 29 applies this promise: the circumcision is God's work and not man's. Paul's phrase 'by the Spirit' describes how the promise is carried out.

The name of the LORD is blasphemed continually because His people have been taken into captivity. Paul applies it to the Jew in Rome: the way the people behave determines how the nations speak about God.

The people profane God's name among the nations, and God promises to cleanse them, to give a new heart and to put His Spirit within them. The passage gives the movement of Romans 2:24 to 2:29 in a single prophecy, from a name dishonored to a heart renewed by the Spirit.

Jeremiah accuses the people of stealing, adultery and false worship while they stand in the temple, calling it a den of robbers. It shows that Paul's questions in verses 21 and 22 echo a prophetic charge: religious privilege and flagrant sin together.

Israel must not covet or take the silver and gold on the idols of the nations. The command lies behind the pointed question 'You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?' because it was Israel's duty to abhor what the pagans worshiped, not to profit from it.

Paul says that believers are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God, glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh. It gives the Christian form of Romans 2:29 and shows that Paul thought of it as a settled conviction.

Believers were circumcised by Christ in the putting off of the sinful nature, buried with Him in baptism and raised with Him. The inward circumcision of Romans 2 is here tied to the death and resurrection of Jesus.

The church is a letter written by the Spirit on human hearts, not on tablets of stone, and ministers of a new covenant serve 'not of the letter but of the Spirit.' This is the clearest parallel to the letter and Spirit contrast of verse 29, and it explains why the letter alone cannot give life.

Abraham was credited with righteousness before he was circumcised, so that he is father of all who believe, circumcised or not. This is the positive side of Romans 2:25 to 29, and it answers the question of what circumcision was for: a seal and not a ground.

Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything; what counts is a new creation. It restates verses 28 and 29 as a principle of the new age: the outward marks of Jew and Gentile give way to the inward reality of regeneration.

study.oneStory:
God called Abraham so that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and the sign of circumcision marked the people through whom the blessing would come. Israel was meant to be 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation,' Exodus 19:6, a people who would show the nations what the true God is like. This passage is where Paul asks what became of that calling.

The history of Israel is told in the Bible with honesty. At Sinai the people made a calf. In the land they did what was right in their own eyes, Judges 21:25. The kings multiplied wrong, and the prophets called for circumcised hearts. The exile that came was the nation being cast out of the land because of the covenant curses they had called on themselves. In exile the name of God was blasphemed among the nations, Ezekiel 36:20, and that is what Paul recalls in verse 24. It is a bitter irony: the people called to display God's character displayed the opposite.

But the same prophets promised a remedy. Jeremiah 31:31-34 announced a new covenant in which the law would be written on the heart and sins forgiven, and Ezekiel 36:26-27 promised a new heart and a new Spirit. These are the promises that stand behind the words 'by the Spirit' in verse 29. The story does not end in exile. It points to a work in which God does for His people what they could not do.

That work arrives in Jesus. He is the faithful Israelite who obeys, the Servant who becomes a light to the nations, the temple that is raised, and the one who pours out the Spirit at Pentecost, Acts 2:33. The circumcision of the heart, which the Law commanded and the Prophets promised, becomes a reality in His people. Because it is no longer tied to a particular nation, the family of Abraham grows to include Gentiles, Galatians 3:28-29, and Ephesians 2:11-22 describes how the wall that divided those who were called 'the circumcision' from those called 'the uncircumcision' has been broken down.

The new creation completes the picture. The holy city has gates 'inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel' and foundations 'bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb,' Revelation 21:12-14, so that the old people and the new gather in one city. Those who stand before the throne are 'from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' Revelation 5:9, 'a kingdom and priests to serve our God,' Revelation 5:10, the calling given at Sinai now fulfilled. The praise that comes from God, which Paul says is what the true Jew receives, is finally given when the Lord says, 'Well done, good and faithful servant,' Matthew 25:21.

quiz.q: What advantages does Paul grant to the person who calls himself a Jew?

options.text: He relies on the law, boasts in God, knows His will, and is instructed by the law.
options.note: Verses 17 and 18 list exactly these real, God-given privileges.

options.text: He possesses the law and genuine knowledge of God's revealed will.
options.note: True as far as it goes, though Paul's list is fuller, including boasting in God and guiding others.

options.text: He is automatically righteous before God because of his ancestry.
options.note: Paul grants privileges but denies that they make anyone righteous apart from obedience.

options.text: He has no advantage of any kind over the Gentiles.
options.note: Paul affirms real advantages here, and states them plainly again in 3:1-2.

quiz.q: What is the sharp contradiction Paul exposes in verses 21 to 23?

options.text: The one who teaches and boasts in the law dishonors God by breaking it.
options.note: Paul's questions expose the gap between teaching the law and keeping it.

options.text: The teacher of the law fails to practice what he preaches to others.
options.note: Accurate, though the fuller point is that this breaking of the law dishonors God.

options.text: The Jew teaches the law too strictly for others to follow.
options.note: Paul's charge is not strictness but hypocrisy, teaching what he does not do.

options.text: The Jew refuses to teach the law to the Gentiles at all.
options.note: The problem is not withholding teaching but failing to live it out.

quiz.q: According to Paul, what happens to circumcision if a person breaks the law?

options.text: His circumcision has become uncircumcision; the outward sign counts as nothing.
options.note: Verse 25 states this directly: lawbreaking empties the sign of value.

options.text: The sign loses its worth because obedience, not the mark, is what matters.
options.note: Correct in principle; the text puts it more starkly as circumcision becoming uncircumcision.

options.text: His circumcision still guarantees his standing regardless of his conduct.
options.note: The reverse of Paul's argument; the sign without obedience is worthless.

options.text: Circumcision was never of any value to anyone at any time.
options.note: Paul says it has value if you observe the law; the problem is lawbreaking.

quiz.q: How does Paul define the true Jew and true circumcision?

options.text: A Jew inwardly, whose circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code.
options.note: Verse 29 gives precisely this inward, Spirit-wrought definition.

options.text: One whose heart is changed within rather than merely marked outwardly.
options.note: Right in substance, though it omits the key phrase by the Spirit, not by the written code.

options.text: One who keeps the ceremonial law more carefully than others.
options.note: Paul locates true circumcision in the heart by the Spirit, not in ceremonial rigor.

options.text: Anyone born into the nation of Israel, without exception.
options.note: Paul explicitly denies that a man is a Jew merely because he is one outwardly.

quiz.q: Whose praise does the truly circumcised person receive?

options.text: Praise from God, not from men.
options.note: Verse 29 ends exactly here: such a man's praise comes from God, not men.

options.text: Approval from God rather than the applause of people.
options.note: Correct in meaning; the text states it as praise from God, not from men.

options.text: Recognition from the religious community for his obedience.
options.note: Paul contrasts God's praise with human recognition, not centers it there.

options.text: No praise at all, since God never commends anyone.
options.note: The verse says the opposite: his praise comes from God.

questions: Paul lists real privileges the Jew enjoyed, yet warns they could not save. What spiritual advantages or knowledge might you be quietly resting in instead of resting in Christ?
The teacher who preached against stealing was stealing. Where is there a gap between what you tell others is right and what you actually practice?
God's name can be dishonored among outsiders by the inconsistency of His people. How might your daily conduct be shaping the way others think about God?
Paul says true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit. What is the difference between outward religious activity and an inwardly changed heart, and which describes you?
The truly transformed person seeks praise from God rather than from people. Whose approval are you actually living for this week?

translationNotes.note: God's name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you draws on Isaiah 52:5. Paul turns the lament into an indictment: Israel's disobedience causes the nations to speak against God.

By the Spirit, not by the written code translates a contrast between pneuma and gramma. The phrase can be read as by the Spirit rather than the letter, pointing to the inward, Spirit-wrought reality of the new covenant.
